standard.title: Implement modular programs with OOP
standard.description: implement, modify and debug modular programs, applying selected algorithms and data structures, including in an object-oriented programming language
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can implement, modify and debug programs involving control structures and functions (AC9TDI8P09). They have experience with iteration, selection, and basic functions. They have not yet implemented programs across multiple files or classes, applied data structures beyond simple lists, or written object-oriented code with custom classes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students implement, modify and debug modular programs using selected algorithms and data structures, including defining and using custom classes in an object-oriented programming language.

nodes.label: Applying data structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and use appropriate data structures (arrays, dictionaries, objects) to model structured data in their programs.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one data structure beyond a simple variable (e.g. list/array or dictionary) to store and access structured data in a program.
nodes.typical_width: Select appropriate data structures for different data needs — arrays for ordered sequential data, dictionaries/records for key-value data, objects for structured entities; justify the selection; access and manipulate stored data using the appropriate operations.
wider: Apply the binary search algorithm from a library to search sorted data — explain why binary search is faster than linear search and what preconditions it requires
Use multiple data structures in the same program and explain what each is responsible for modelling
Investigate how choosing the wrong data structure (e.g. using a list when a dictionary is needed) affects program complexity and performance

response_modes.reason: Data structure selection requires students to reason about the shape of the data and how it will be accessed. Students default to lists for everything. Multiple varied scenarios — ordered lists, character stats in RPGs, temperature records — each foreground a different data structure choice.

success_criteria: Program uses a data structure with more than one element
Student can explain why that data structure suits the data being stored
nodes.hinge_reason: Data structure selection errors propagate through all subsequent nodes — a student who uses a list where a dictionary is needed produces a program at N5 that is structurally incorrect and cannot be cleanly extended or debugged.

nodes.label: Defining custom classes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define a custom class with attributes and methods that models an entity in their program.
nodes.minimum_width: Define a class with at least two attributes and one method; create at least one instance of the class and call the method.
nodes.typical_width: Define a class that models a real entity (e.g. book, character, sensor reading) with appropriate attributes and methods; create multiple instances; use the class to represent structured data in a program.
wider: Define a class with methods that track and modify the object's state over time — e.g. a library book class with methods to check out, return and reserve
Design and implement a class hierarchy with at least one subclass — explain what inheritance achieves and when it is and isn't appropriate
Refactor an existing program that uses dictionaries or parallel lists to use a custom class — explain what the refactor improves

response_modes.reason: OOP syntax and concepts require substantial practice. Students commonly confuse class definitions with instances, mix up self and instance variables, or misplace method definitions. Fluency with basic class definition and instantiation is a prerequisite for modular program design.

success_criteria: Class definition includes at least two attributes and one method with correct syntax
At least one instance is created and the method is successfully called
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot define a class correctly cannot read or modify class-based code at N3, and cannot implement a modular OOP program at N5 — class syntax fluency is directly prerequisite.

nodes.label: Reading and modifying modular programs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can read and interpret programs split across multiple functions, files or classes, and modify them to add functionality.
nodes.minimum_width: Read a provided modular program (split across files or functions); identify what each module does; make one modification that adds or changes functionality.
nodes.typical_width: Read a program split across files, functions and/or classes; trace execution flow across modules; make modifications that add new functionality without breaking existing behaviour; explain how the modular structure made the modification easier.
wider: Extend a provided game codebase (e.g. an adventure game) by adding new characters, levels or abilities — identify where in the existing structure each addition belongs
Investigate how large codebases manage module dependencies and explain what problems arise when modules are tightly coupled
success_criteria: Correctly identifies what at least two modules/functions/classes do in a provided codebase
Makes a modification that works correctly without breaking existing functionality

nodes.label: Debugging programs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate a bug in a program by reading error messages, printing variable state, and tracing execution; modify the program to fix the bug and verify the fix.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a program with a bug, identify the location of the error by reading the error message or printing variable values; explain what caused it; fix it and test the fix.
nodes.typical_width: Debug a program with at least two bugs using a systematic approach — read error messages, print or inspect variable state, trace execution, locate the cause, apply fix, test; document the debugging process.
wider: Debug a program where the error is a logic error (produces wrong output without crashing) rather than a syntax or runtime error — explain why logic errors are harder to find
Investigate and fix a bug in a larger modular program where the cause and symptom are in different modules

response_modes.reason: Debugging is systematic reasoning under uncertainty — students who guess at fixes without understanding the cause often make things worse. A structured approach (read error → form hypothesis about cause → test hypothesis by printing state → apply fix → verify) is the key skill and must be explicitly scaffolded.

success_criteria: Identifies the location of the bug (not just the symptom)
Explains the cause of the bug before applying the fix
Verifies the fix produces correct output
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who guess at bug fixes without diagnosis cannot complete N5 — a modular program will always have bugs, and students who cannot systematically locate and explain bugs before fixing them produce programs with unfixed or newly introduced errors.

nodes.label: Implementing a complete modular program
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write and edit a modular program that receives structured input, applies algorithms and data structures, and produces correct output.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a program that uses at least one custom class or function and processes structured input to produce output; the program produces correct output for a test input.
nodes.typical_width: Implement a program that is split into logical modules (functions and/or classes); the program processes structured input, applies appropriate data structures and algorithms, and produces correct output for the problem; test with multiple inputs.
wider: Write a program that reads structured data from a file (e.g. timestamped sensor data) and processes it to produce an output — such as a graph of an altitude sensor's flight path
Build a program that models a real inventory, library or tracking system using custom classes — implement the required methods to track state changes over time
Use a data structure from a library (e.g. binary search function) in a program and explain why using the library is preferable to reimplementing from scratch

response_modes.reason: Nodes 1–4 cover data structures, classes, reading modular code, and debugging separately. Implementation requires all of these simultaneously — choosing data structures, defining classes, organising modules, and debugging when things go wrong. Students who can do each individually often struggle when they must design the whole program architecture.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: File-based input processing and real system simulation (inventory/library) are rich directions — they require students to handle real data formats and design modular architecture that reflects domain requirements. These are substantive programming projects.
success_criteria: Program is split into at least two logical modules (functions or classes)
Program produces correct output for at least two different test inputs
Program handles at least one edge case without crashing
